newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. Mideast envoy going home without Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mideast envoy going home without Hebron deal.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's special peace envoy is leaving the Middle East, having failed to close a deal on the West Bank town of Hebron in Israeli-PLO talks that the Palestinians said were nearing a dead end.
U.S. embassy spokesman Richard Scorza told Reuters on Sunday: "Dennis Ross will leave tonight. He feels that the mediation role has been achieved, the assignment is complete."
Asked if Ross's mission had failed for lack of an agreement, Scorza said: "It's up to the parties to make the deal."
Ross arrived three weeks ago to try again to forge a deal to launch Palestinian self-rule in 80 percent of the Israeli-occupied West Bank town, a flashpoint of Arab-Israeli violence.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's cabinet charged late on Saturday that the talks with Israel had reached a crisis, saying in a statement: "The talks are close to a dead end."

Ross said in Cairo on Saturday that the outstanding issues for the most part did not concern Hebron at all. The talks have hit an impasse over a timetable for planned Israeli withdrawals following the Hebron pullback.

Israel was due to have completed the Hebron handover 10 months ago. But violence, security concerns, and other issues have held up a deal. Some 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs live in the town, holy to both as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
Jordan's King Hussein and his prime minister, Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, were due in self-ruled Gaza later on Sunday to meet Arafat.

"This is part of the Jordanian-Egyptian-Palestinian consultation on the peace process," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters. The trip is King Hussein's first to the Gaza Strip since Israel seized it in the 1967 Middle East war.
"If the international community does not move immediately to save the peace process...then the whole region will witness explosions," Arafat's cabinet said in its statement on Saturday.

It said Israel was violating its 1995 interim peace deal with the Palestine Liberation Organisation by demanding that future withdrawals, due to be completed in largely rural areas by September 1997, be put off until May 1999.
Palestinians have rejected a U.S. compromise proposal that Israel complete further West Bank withdrawals by 1998.

In Jerusalem, Ross held late-night talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Earlier he reported no breakthroughs in meetings with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Palestinian negotiators in Cairo.

On a one-day trip to Paris at the weekend, Arafat urged French President Jacques Chirac to add a European dimension to peace moves. Arafat held talks with a European Union special envoy upon returning to Gaza on Saturday.
Palestinian officials have been grumbling about U.S. "bias" in Israel's favour in the talks. Negotiator Saeb Erekat said he did not anticipate a quick resolution of the impasse.
"The main sticking point is not something easy. It is the nucleus of the interim agreement. It is the further redeployments," he told reporters in Cairo.

"The second Mr Netanyahu makes up his mind and gives his negotiator the green light to stick to the agreement signed in Washington...I think we will move to implement the outstanding commitments in the agreement," Erekat said.
